facts.statement: 50 failed logins for j.doe@example.com from 203.0.113.45, then a successful login from the same IP at 2026-11-23T03:13:51Z (15s after the last failure).
203.0.113.45 has no history for j.doe@example.com in the searched look-back (2026-10-24 to 2026-11-23): the IP is new for this account.
203.0.113.45 also targeted 2 other account(s) in the same window: a.kumar@example.com (12 failed, 0 successful), m.lee@example.com (8 failed, 0 successful).
After the login, the same IP session performed: file_access, logout, mailbox_rule_created.
A mailbox rule forwarding mail to an external address (ext.billing-update@example.org) was created at 2026-11-23T03:17:03Z.
Files were read from \\fs-fin-01\payables (14 files, 8421377 bytes) at 2026-11-23T03:21:31Z.
Logins used a scripted client user agent (python-requests/2.31), not a browser or mail app.
j.doe@example.com is not enrolled in MFA (a password alone was enough to log in).
Login at 03:13 UTC is outside usual hours 03:30-12:30; 203.0.113.45 is not one of the account's usual IPs.
WS-FIN-014 is a high-criticality Accounts payable workstation (Finance).
MOCK intel rates 203.0.113.45 as malicious (score 87, tags credential-stuffing, password-spray).

reasons: F1: brute force followed by a successful login (account access likely obtained)
F5: external mail-forwarding rule created after the login
F6 + F10: files read from a share using a high-criticality asset
all key facts were checked and every tool call succeeded
F11 comes from MOCK intel; it supports the conclusion but is not relied on alone

assessment.what_likely_happened: An external actor at 203.0.113.45 ran an automated password-guessing/spray campaign against example.com accounts, including j.doe@example.com, and succeeded on the first target after 50 failures in ~15 minutes (F1, F3, F7). The account had no MFA, so the password alone yielded a session (F8). The same session then acted like a hands-on intruder: it created an external mail-forwarding rule to ext.billing-update@example.org and read 14 files (approx. 8.4 MB) from the \\fs-fin-01\payables share on a high-criticality Accounts Payable workstation (F4, F5, F6, F10). The login was 15s after the last failure, from an IP never before seen for this account, using a python-requests client rather than a browser or mail app, and outside the account's usual hours (F1, F2, F7, F9). This pattern is consistent with successful brute force/password spraying leading to credential misuse, email collection via forwarding rule, and staging of financial data — i.e., likely business email compromise plus data theft from Finance.

hypotheses.explanation: 50 failures followed 15 seconds later by success from the same IP (F1), with an IP never seen for this account (F2), a scripted python-requests client (F7), no MFA enrolled so password alone sufficed (F8), and an out-of-hours login from a non-usual IP (F9). Post-login actions — external mail-forwarding rule and reading 14 payables files (F4, F5, F6) — are inconsistent with a normal interactive user session and consistent with hands-on use of a guessed credential.

A legitimate user mistyping a password would use a browser or mail client, not python-requests/2.31 (F7), and would not generate 50 failures across a 15-minute window while also hitting two other accounts (F3). A real user would not create a forwarding rule to an external billing-looking address and bulk-read payables share files immediately after logging in (F5, F6), and the IP is entirely new to this account (F2).

Nothing in the facts positively establishes insider or delegated activity versus external attack — attribution is a gap. However, the same IP also sprayed two other accounts (F3), a scripted client was used (F7), and the failure-then-success sequence at 15s (F1) fits automation, which weakens a stale-password/retry-loop explanation. The facts do not, by themselves, disprove insider involvement.

The same source IP attempted 12 logins on a.kumar@example.com and 8 on m.lee@example.com in the same window with no success (F3), while succeeding only on j.doe after 50 attempts (F1) using an automated client (F7) — the classic spray/credential-stuffing pattern where one account is the confirmed success.

Post-login activity is already malicious in nature: an external mail-forwarding rule (F5) — a persistence/collection mechanism — plus reads of 14 files from a payables share (F6) on a high-criticality Finance workstation (F10), preceded by file_access and logout events from the same session (F4). Further lateral movement or persistence beyond these facts is not evidenced and remains an unknown.

alternative_explanations.explanation: A security test, pen-test, or automated integration/credential-rotation script owned by Finance IT that legitimately uses python-requests and touched a payables share.
alternative_explanations.why_less_likely: The source IP also failed logins against two unrelated accounts (F3), created a forwarding rule to an external non-corporate-looking domain (F5), and is new to the account and outside the user's normal hours/IPs (F2, F9) — sanctioned testing would normally be allow-listed and coordinated with the affected account holders.

alternative_explanations.explanation: A compromised or malicious on-host tool shared by a third party (e.g., a vendor script running on the workstation) minting sessions for the finance user.
alternative_explanations.why_less_likely: The 50-failure burst then success 15 seconds later from a single external IP never seen before for the account (F1, F2) with an unenrolled-MFA login (F8) is more characteristic of an external guessing campaign than local tooling, and the external forwarding destination (F5) points outward.

unknowns: Whether other accounts beyond a.kumar and m.lee were targeted or compromised by 203.0.113.45 — failed/success counts were only reported for three accounts.
What the 14 payables files contain and whether data actually left the network after the mailbox rule was created (exfiltration not observed in the facts).
Whether the external forwarding address ext.billing-update@example.org received any mail and whether it is a known attacker mailbox or related infrastructure.
Whether the attacker performed further actions beyond file_access, logout, and mailbox_rule_created — full session/telemetry for WS-FIN-014 and any other hosts is not represented in the facts.
Whether lateral movement to other Finance hosts or privileged accounts occurred using j.doe's session or password (F4 shows only these three events).
How the password was obtained (guessed vs. leaked/stuffed) — the facts show the pattern but not the source of the credential.
Whether j.doe was aware of or involved in the activity (insider possibility unresolved).
Attribution: 203.0.113.45 is not established as external/foreign infrastructure beyond the mock intel (F11), and mock intel is not relied on alone.

severity_view.explanation: If true, the impact is maxed out: an external actor got a valid session on a high-criticality Accounts Payable workstation (F1, F10) without MFA (F8), created an external mail-forwarding rule for persistent email collection (F5), and read 14 payables files from a Finance share (F6) — the combination of account takeover, email exfiltration setup, and sensitive financial data access justifies critical. I agree with the rubric; the only caveat is that actual data exfiltration is not evidenced in the facts, so the harm is 'access + collection staging' rather than confirmed loss, which does not lower the level given the asset criticality.
